title: A Pigeon's Compass in Its Liver
hook: The clue to how pigeons find their way home may be hiding in the liver: iron-packed immune cells that could act like tiny magnetic sensors.
key_points: Researchers found iron-filled immune cells in pigeon livers that may sense magnetism.
Birds without these cells struggled to navigate home under overcast skies.
That suggests they fall back on Earth's magnetic field when the sun is hidden.
The finding hints at a surprising link between the immune system and sensing.
content_html: How do homing pigeons find their way back over unfamiliar terrain? Part of the answer may be hiding somewhere unexpected — the liver. Scientists report, via ScienceDaily, that they found iron-filled immune cells there that may act like tiny magnetic sensors, letting the bird read Earth's magnetic field like a built-in compass.
extra_html: The key test came on cloudy days. When the sun was hidden, pigeons that lacked these iron-rich cells struggled to find their way home, while normal birds managed — evidence that they lean on the magnetic field for guidance when other cues, like the sun, aren't available. Beyond possibly cracking a decades-old mystery about how animals navigate, the discovery hints at a stranger link: that the immune system, usually thought of as the body's defense force, might also play a role in sensing the outside world. The researchers present it as a promising lead rather than a closed case.
